paragraphs: Coordinate descent improves an objective by updating individual coordinates. Greedy versions choose coordinates according to their immediate promise, but combining that choice with acceleration raises theoretical challenges. This paper introduces two methods, Accelerated Semi-Greedy Coordinate Descent (ASCD) and Accelerated Greedy Coordinate Descent (AGCD), to investigate both provable convergence and practical performance.

The strongest general theoretical results concern ASCD. The authors establish an O(1/k²) convergence rate and accelerated linear convergence for strongly convex functions. In numerical experiments, both proposed methods outperform Accelerated Randomized Coordinate Descent on most instances. AGCD performs substantially better than the other two methods in those experiments, despite lacking the same general theoretical guarantees.

The paper examines this gap between observed behavior and available proofs. It explains why standard acceleration proof techniques cannot establish the desired result for AGCD, then identifies a technical condition that does guarantee accelerated convergence. That condition holds in the reported experiments. The contribution therefore combines a theoretically supported method with a stronger empirical performer whose acceleration receives a conditional justification.
icml-2018-accelerating-greedy-coordinate.tldr: Two accelerated greedy coordinate methods offer complementary theoretical and empirical strengths, with AGCD’s acceleration guaranteed under a stated technical condition.

paragraphs: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning models a human and robot working toward a shared objective whose reward parameters only the human knows. The robot must infer those parameters during interaction. Earlier work expressed this problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, but the resulting action space grew exponentially with the reward parameter space.

The paper exploits the human’s access to full information to modify the Bellman update, the calculation used to evaluate decisions through their future consequences. This modification preserves optimality while reducing complexity by an exponential factor. It also supports relaxing the model’s assumption that the human acts rationally, extending the framework beyond that original behavioral assumption.

The authors incorporate the update into exact, point-based, and Monte Carlo Tree Search solvers. They report solving larger problems with more reward parameters and more actions for both participants. In these solutions, human behavior can deliberately teach the robot about the objective, and the robot interprets it accordingly. This produces higher value for the human in the studied interactions.
icml-2018-an-efficient-generalized-bellm.tldr: A modified Bellman update preserves CIRL optimality while reducing complexity exponentially and enabling larger human–robot cooperation problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a signal from noisy measurements that retain amplitude information but lose phase. It formulates recovery as a nonconvex optimization problem with an ℓ₂ regularization term and develops a message passing algorithm intended to solve it. The central question is how accurately this algorithm recovers signals as measurement availability and noise change.

The analysis considers an asymptotic regime: both the number of measurements m and signal dimension n grow without bound, while their ratio approaches a fixed value. Within this setting, the authors obtain sharp performance bounds. For complex signals, they show that accurate recovery is possible with m = (64/π² − 4)n, approximately 2.5 measurements per signal dimension. They also characterize sensitivity to noise.

Two findings clarify the algorithm’s behavior. Adding ℓ₂ regularization can help even when the observations contain no noise, so its value here extends beyond handling measurement corruption. Spectral initialization has only a marginal effect on performance. Together, these results connect algorithm design choices to recovery behavior under the paper’s asymptotic analysis.
icml-2018-approximate-message-passing-fo.tldr: An asymptotic analysis of message passing establishes sharp phaseless recovery bounds and shows that regularization can help even without noise.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization addresses objectives that are expensive to evaluate and whose internal workings are unavailable. When evaluations can run in parallel, the optimizer must choose a batch of inputs rather than a single next input. This paper proposes constructing that batch by considering several acquisition functions together, allowing multiple criteria to shape the search.

At each iteration, the method treats the acquisition functions as separate objectives in a multi-objective optimization problem. It searches for their Pareto front: candidate inputs representing trade-offs where improving one acquisition objective would require sacrificing another. The batch is then selected from this front. This gives a concrete way to turn disagreement among acquisition functions into a collection of evaluation candidates.

The authors assess the approach using analytical benchmark functions and real analog integrated circuit design problems, comparing it with several established batch Bayesian optimization methods. The reported results are competitive with those alternatives. The approach can improve optimization efficiency by using parallel evaluations to explore trade-offs among acquisition criteria, rather than requiring one acquisition function to determine the entire batch.
icml-2018-batch-bayesian-optimization-vi.tldr: The method selects parallel Bayesian optimization evaluations from trade-offs among multiple acquisition functions, with competitive benchmark and circuit-design results.

paragraphs: This paper uses numerical differential equations to guide neural network architecture design. It interprets ResNet, PolyNet, FractalNet, and RevNet as different numerical discretizations of differential equations. That connection makes established ideas for approximating continuous dynamics available as principles for constructing deep networks, providing a mathematical perspective on architectural choices.

As a concrete example, the authors introduce a linear multi-step architecture inspired by methods for solving ordinary differential equations. Applied to ResNet and ResNeXt, it achieves higher accuracy on CIFAR and ImageNet with comparable numbers of trainable parameters. They also report compressing the original networks by more than 50% while retaining similar performance, and explain this behavior through the numerical-analysis concept of a modified equation.

The paper additionally connects noise injection during training with stochastic control. Relating stochastic training to stochastic dynamical systems provides a route for applying such training to the proposed architecture. Adding stochastic depth to LM-ResNet improves its CIFAR10 performance in the reported experiment. The work therefore contributes both an architecture and a broader mathematical basis for designing and training related networks.
icml-2018-beyond-finite-layer-neural-net.tldr: Interpreting neural networks as numerical differential-equation methods inspires a multi-step architecture with improved accuracy and substantial compression in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse regression methods such as the Lasso seek solutions using relatively few features, but optimizing them in high dimensions can be expensive. Existing acceleration strategies reduce the active problem by screening out irrelevant features or concentrating on features likely to receive nonzero coefficients. This paper improves the information used to make those decisions.

The key technique constructs better dual points by extrapolating from a sequence of dual iterates. Dual information helps assess how close the current solution is to optimality. Improving it therefore tightens the control used in stopping criteria and strengthens the performance of Gap Safe screening rules. The same construction supports both deciding when optimization is sufficiently complete and reducing the features that still need attention.

The authors combine this technique with a working set strategy that makes aggressive use of Gap Safe screening. They report significant computational speedups across multiple real-world problems. The contribution links better optimality information to more effective allocation of solver effort: improved dual points help the algorithm focus computation on a smaller, more relevant optimization problem.
icml-2018-celer-a-fast-solver-for-the-la.tldr: Celer accelerates Lasso optimization by constructing better dual points that improve stopping criteria, feature screening, and working set selection.

paragraphs: Caching requires deciding which items to evict before future requests are known. Learned predictions may help, but following them directly can perform badly even when their average error is small. This paper develops a framework for incorporating a learned oracle into online algorithms while preserving protection against unreliable advice.

For a cache of size k, the authors modify the Marker algorithm to use oracle predictions. The resulting competitive ratio improves as prediction error decreases and remains bounded by O(log k), the guarantee available without predictions. A competitive ratio measures performance relative to an optimal benchmark, so the result connects the benefit of accurate advice with a fallback guarantee when advice is poor.

The framework treats the oracle as a black box and does not depend on its internal implementation or the precise distribution of its errors. Experiments on real-world datasets show good performance even with simple off-the-shelf predictors. The central contribution is a way to benefit from learned information without allowing prediction mistakes to remove the algorithm’s stated worst-case protection.
icml-2018-competitive-caching-with-machi.tldr: A prediction-aware caching algorithm improves with accurate advice while retaining an O(log k) competitive guarantee when predictions are unreliable.

paragraphs: Deep probabilistic models can represent complex functions, but modeling tasks may also impose knowledge about how those functions should behave. This paper introduces a generative framework for expressing such knowledge as soft constraints. The constraints can involve function values or derivatives of a specified order, and can take either equality or inequality form.

The authors use stochastic variational inference to characterize a posterior distribution over both model parameters and constraint parameters. This keeps uncertainty about the constrained model within the probabilistic formulation. The approach is intended to provide accurate, scalable uncertainty quantification for predictions as well as for all parameters, while retaining flexibility in the functions being modeled.

Two applications illustrate the different kinds of constraints. Equality constraints support parameter inference in ordinary differential equation models, where the modeled dynamics encode relationships to be satisfied. Inequality constraints support monotonic regression of count data, where behavior is restricted in direction. Across several experimental settings, the authors report highly competitive results, showing how behavioral knowledge and expressive probabilistic modeling can be combined within one inference framework.
icml-2018-constraining-the-dynamics-of-d.tldr: A probabilistic framework incorporates soft equality and inequality constraints on functions and derivatives while estimating uncertainty through variational inference.

paragraphs: Incorrect class labels complicate training because a neural network receives misleading supervision alongside useful examples. This paper studies the problem through the dimensionality of the representations learned for training samples. Its focus is the geometry of the network’s internal representation subspaces and how that geometry changes when some labels are wrong.

The authors find distinctive dimensionality-related learning behavior when comparing training with clean labels against training with a proportion of noisy labels. They turn that observation into a training strategy: monitor subspace dimensionality during learning and adapt the loss function accordingly. Representation geometry therefore becomes a signal that influences how the model continues to learn, rather than serving only as something examined after training.

Experiments show that the proposed approach tolerates substantial proportions of noisy labels and learns low-dimensional local subspaces that capture the data distribution. These are empirical findings about the studied training strategy. The contribution is a connection between measurable properties of learned representations and an adaptive loss, offering a way to respond to label noise through the network’s evolving internal structure.
icml-2018-dimensionality-driven-learning.tldr: Monitoring learned representation dimensionality and adapting the loss yields strong empirical tolerance to noisy class labels.

paragraphs: Active object tracking requires a system to observe a target and move its camera to keep tracking it. Separately designing the tracking and camera-control components makes joint tuning difficult and can require substantial labeling and real-world trial and error. This paper instead learns a direct mapping from visual observations to camera actions through deep reinforcement learning.

The model combines a convolutional network with an LSTM to predict actions from frame sequences. Training also uses environment augmentation and a customized reward function, both identified as crucial to success. The tracker learns in the ViZDoom and Unreal Engine simulators, placing the acquisition of tracking behavior within controlled simulated environments.

The trained tracker generalizes in the reported tests to unfamiliar target motion, appearances, backgrounds, and distracting objects. It can also regain tracking after occasionally losing its target. Experiments using the VOT dataset suggest that skills learned solely in simulation can potentially transfer to real-world scenarios. That transfer result is presented as evidence of potential, while the simulation tests demonstrate several specific forms of generalization.
icml-2018-end-to-end-active-object-track.tldr: A reinforcement learning tracker maps video directly to camera actions, generalizes across simulated changes, and shows potential for real-world transfer.

paragraphs: Randomized least-squares algorithms make large problems more manageable by computing approximate solutions. A practical difficulty remains: users often cannot tell how far a particular approximation is from the exact solution or how much additional computation would meet their accuracy target. Worst-case bounds may provide only broad guidance for that specific input.

This paper proposes a bootstrap method for estimating error after an approximate solution has been computed. These a posteriori estimates let users assess a solution numerically and predict the work needed to improve a preliminary result. The method thus connects an existing approximate answer with a practical decision about whether further computation is worthwhile.

The authors establish theoretical consistency results and demonstrate effectiveness empirically. They also emphasize flexibility: the method applies to several popular sketching algorithms and multiple error measures, rather than depending on a single solver or definition of accuracy. Its additional computational cost is reported to be small relative to the underlying sketching algorithm. The contribution makes randomized optimization results easier to assess and refine for individual problems.
icml-2018-error-estimation-for-randomize.tldr: A low-overhead bootstrap method estimates the error of randomized least-squares solutions and helps predict the computation needed to improve them.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering can be computationally expensive when a network changes over time, because repeated clustering repeatedly encounters the cost of computing graph eigenvectors. This paper asks how information from earlier cluster assignments can make subsequent clustering faster. The aim is to exploit continuity between successive network states while retaining assignments close in quality to spectral clustering.

The method builds on polynomial-based randomized sketching, which avoids directly computing the eigenvectors that form the main bottleneck. It combines this approach with reuse of information from past assignments. The analysis shows approximate spectral-clustering quality and potential reductions in computational complexity when the graph’s dynamics are appropriately bounded. The benefit therefore has an explicit connection to how the network changes.

In experiments on graphs with 30,000 nodes, the method is 3.9 times faster on average and differs from the correct assignment by less than 0.1%. These results illustrate the practical value of the approach in the tested setting. The broader contribution is a strategy for updating clusters using both a cheaper spectral approximation and information already obtained from earlier network states.
icml-2018-fast-approximate-spectral-clus.tldr: Reusing past assignments with randomized spectral sketches accelerates dynamic graph clustering when graph changes are suitably bounded.

paragraphs: Maximizing area under the ROC curve creates a particular challenge for stochastic learning: the surrogate loss depends on pairs containing a positive and a negative example, while the classical setting reveals only one randomly drawn example per iteration. This paper develops an algorithm that works within that one-example-at-a-time setting.

The approach starts from a saddle point formulation of a consistent square-loss surrogate for AUC. Using that formulation, the authors improve the standard O(1/√n) statistical convergence rate to approximately O(1/n), with a logarithmic factor, where n counts observed samples. The result does not require strong convexity or favorable statistical conditions such as low noise. Those qualifications matter because they identify assumptions the faster rate avoids.

The authors describe this as the first stochastic AUC algorithm with such a rate, to their knowledge. Experiments on eight large-scale benchmark datasets show better performance than existing stochastic or online AUC maximization algorithms. The paper therefore combines a faster statistical guarantee with empirical evidence that its treatment of the pair-dependent objective works effectively in sequential learning.
icml-2018-fast-stochastic-auc-maximizati.tldr: A saddle point approach achieves near-O(1/n) stochastic AUC convergence without strong convexity or favorable noise assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies variance-reduced optimization methods that randomly choose a batch size before selecting samples for each update. It establishes linear convergence for this framework on composite functions. When efficiency is measured purely by data accesses, the best strategy is always choosing a batch of one, which recovers the SAGA algorithm.

The authors then account for the cost of accessing data on actual hardware. Random memory access is slower than sequential access, and disk seeking adds further expense when data does not fit in memory. Under this accounting, minimizing the number of accessed samples does not necessarily minimize running time, and a batch size of one is no longer optimal.

The resulting method, SAGA++, comes with a theoretical calculation of the optimal average batch size. Experiments on real datasets show it outperforming SAGA and other batch and stochastic solvers. A separate comparison of variance-reduction update rules also establishes faster theoretical convergence than SVRG. The paper’s central point is that batch selection should reflect both optimization progress and the architecture-dependent cost of obtaining data.
icml-2018-fast-variance-reduction-method.tldr: SAGA++ chooses batches using memory and disk access costs, improving practical performance beyond the single-sample strategy favored by data-access counts.

paragraphs: Estimating worker skill in crowdsourcing becomes difficult when workers label sparse, irregular subsets of tasks. Under the single-coin Dawid–Skene model, this paper expresses skill estimation as completion of a rank-one correlation matrix. Its observed entries represent label correlations between workers, connecting the estimation problem to the pattern of available worker comparisons.

The authors establish an exact structural characterization: recovery and skill identifiability hold if and only if the sampling matrix is irreducible and aperiodic. For sampling matrices satisfying these conditions, they propose an efficient gradient descent scheme and prove convergence of skill estimates to the desired global optima. The result is notable because weighted rank-one matrix factorization is NP-hard in general.

For noisy observations, the paper derives sample complexity bounds involving spectral properties of the sampling matrix’s signless Laplacian. This ties the amount of evidence required to the structure of worker interactions. The proposed method also achieves state-of-the-art performance on several real-world datasets. Together, the results explain when sparse comparison patterns support recovery and provide an algorithm with guarantees for those patterns.
icml-2018-gradient-descent-for-sparse-ra.tldr: Worker-skill estimation becomes rank-one matrix completion, with exact sampling conditions for identifiability and a convergent gradient descent method.

paragraphs: Nonconvex methods for statistical estimation often use explicit safeguards such as trimming, projection, or regularized objectives to obtain fast-convergence guarantees. For plain gradient descent, earlier theory sometimes required very conservative learning rates or offered no guarantee. This paper explains how gradient descent itself can exhibit a stabilizing effect in several nonconvex estimation problems.

The key finding concerns the path taken by the iterates. Even without explicit regularization, gradient descent stays within a region with favorable geometry whose points remain incoherent with the sampling mechanism. This implicit regularization allows more aggressive progress without overshooting. The explanation links fast convergence to the behavior of the whole optimization trajectory, rather than to an added corrective step.

The authors establish near-optimal statistical and computational guarantees for random quadratic systems and low-rank matrix completion. For noisy matrix completion, they additionally obtain optimal control of entrywise errors and spectral-norm error. These conclusions concern the studied statistical problems. They show why explicit regularization can be unnecessary for strong guarantees in these settings and why plain gradient descent can save substantial computation.
icml-2018-implicit-regularization-in-non.tldr: In the studied nonconvex estimation problems, gradient descent implicitly stays in favorable regions and achieves strong guarantees without explicit regularization.

paragraphs: Variational auto-encoders use inference networks to estimate distributions over hidden variables from observations. Learning this mapping shares inference effort across examples, making inference computationally efficient. However, a direct prediction can fall short of the approximate posterior obtainable through fuller optimization. The difference is known as the amortization gap.

This paper proposes iterative inference models that learn how to refine their estimates through repeated encoding of gradients. Instead of producing an approximate posterior in a single direct mapping, the model learns an optimization process that updates the estimate. The approach generalizes standard VAE inference networks and aims to reduce the gap between fast learned inference and more fully optimized approximate posteriors.

The authors demonstrate that these models can perform inference optimization and outperform standard inference networks on several image and text benchmarks. The framework also offers insight into empirical findings involving top-down inference techniques. Its main contribution is to make iterative improvement part of learned inference itself, retaining the idea of sharing computation across examples while allowing each posterior estimate to be progressively refined.
icml-2018-iterative-amortized-inference-.tldr: Iterative inference networks repeatedly encode gradients to refine approximate posteriors and outperform standard direct inference models on image and text benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper considers learning representations that third parties will later use for prediction, even when their objectives are unknown during representation training. The goal is to reduce unfair downstream outcomes while preserving useful information. The authors investigate adversarial representation learning as a way to build fairness considerations into the representation before those later tasks are chosen.

A central contribution connects different adversarial objectives to demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity. These are distinct group-fairness criteria, so the training objective determines which fairness behavior the method supports. Worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation show that choosing the adversarial objective is consequential; adversarial training alone does not specify a single interchangeable notion of fairness.

The paper also studies transfer to new prediction tasks. Its experiments show that the learned representations can support fair predictions while maintaining utility on those tasks. This provides empirical evidence for the intended use by downstream users. The contribution combines an analysis of objective choice with a demonstration that fairness-oriented representations can retain value beyond the task used to learn them.
icml-2018-learning-adversarially-fair-an.tldr: The paper links adversarial objectives to specific group-fairness criteria and empirically shows useful, fair transfer to new prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent and matching pursuit both improve an objective by moving along selected directions. Coordinate descent uses coordinate directions, while matching pursuit allows a more general collection. This paper develops a common analysis of these methods and their randomized variants, using their shared structure to relate results that might otherwise be studied separately.

The analysis is affine invariant, expressing convergence in a way that respects changes in the problem’s coordinate representation. It establishes O(1/t) sublinear rates for smooth objectives and linear convergence for strongly convex objectives. As a consequence of the matching-pursuit analysis, the authors also obtain what they describe as the tightest known rates for steepest coordinate descent.

The paper further establishes an accelerated O(1/t²) convergence rate for matching pursuit and steepest coordinate descent on convex objectives, presented as the first such result. The assumptions attached to these rates distinguish the conclusions: smoothness, convexity, and strong convexity support different guarantees. The contribution is both a unified mathematical treatment and stronger convergence results obtained through that connection.
icml-2018-on-matching-pursuit-and-coordi.tldr: A unified affine-invariant analysis connects matching pursuit and coordinate descent and establishes accelerated O(1/t²) convergence on convex objectives.

paragraphs: Estimating a parameter of interest often requires first estimating other, potentially complex nuisance quantities. Double machine learning uses Neyman-orthogonal moment equations to reduce sensitivity to errors in those quantities. First-order orthogonality allows root-n-consistent estimation of the target even when nuisance estimates converge at the slower n⁻¹/⁴ rate.

This paper extends the idea to higher-order orthogonality. With a k-th order notion, the required nuisance rate becomes n⁻¹/(2k+2), allowing slower nuisance estimation while retaining the target estimation guarantee. The result identifies a route to greater robustness when nuisance components are more complex or higher dimensional: suppress sensitivity to additional orders of estimation error.

The paper also identifies a precise boundary in partially linear regression, a setting used in causal inference. Second-order orthogonal moments can be constructed if and only if the treatment residual is not normally distributed. The proof uses Stein’s lemma. An explicit doubly orthogonal treatment-effect procedure demonstrates robustness benefits, while the distributional condition shows that access to higher-order protection depends on the structure of the problem.
icml-2018-orthogonal-machine-learning-po.tldr: Higher-order orthogonality tolerates slower nuisance estimation, but second-order construction in partially linear regression requires nonnormal treatment residuals.

paragraphs: PDE-Net addresses two goals together: forecasting the dynamics of a complex system and discovering the partial differential equation underlying those dynamics. The motivation is that increasingly abundant observations can support learning physical models from data. The proposed feed-forward network learns both differential operators and the nonlinear response function of the governing equation.

Its distinguishing feature is a set of carefully designed constraints on network filters. These constraints connect the order of differential operators with the order of filter sum rules, drawing on a concept from wavelet theory. They make the learned components identifiable as parts of a PDE while preserving the network’s capacity to represent and predict complex behavior.

Numerical experiments show potential to uncover hidden governing equations and predict dynamics over relatively long periods, including in noisy environments. The stated evidence supports that potential rather than a universal discovery guarantee. The approach matters because its architecture supports interpretation and prediction within the same learned model: the filters help connect what the network computes to the mathematical structure of the system’s dynamics.
icml-2018-pde-net-learning-pdes-from-dat.tldr: PDE-Net constrains learned filters to jointly predict system dynamics and identify potential governing PDEs, with promising numerical results under noise.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening replaces a large graph with a smaller representation, making it important to understand which mathematical properties survive that reduction. This paper focuses on the graph Laplacian’s spectrum. It provides conditions under which principal eigenvalues and eigenspaces of the smaller graph remain close to those of the original graph.

The quality of the approximation depends on recognizable graph properties, including degree distributions and eigenvalue distributions. It also depends on the size of the coarsened graph relative to the original. These dependencies connect the reliability of the smaller representation to both the graph’s structure and the amount of reduction, rather than treating all coarsening choices as equivalent.

For spectral clustering, the results imply that eigenvectors computed on the coarse graph can yield good cluster assignments without an additional refinement stage under the relevant conditions. This gives formal support to a phenomenon previously observed in practice. The contribution helps explain when learning methods can use a smaller graph while retaining the spectral information that their outputs depend on.
icml-2018-spectrally-approximating-large.tldr: The paper gives conditions for graph coarsening to preserve key spectral information and support good clustering assignments without refinement.

paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box objective becomes difficult when candidate inputs have rich structure, such as combinations of Gaussian-process kernels. This paper uses the Automatic Statistician as a case study for turning that structured search into a continuous optimization problem. A Structure Generating Variational Auto-encoder embeds kernel combinations into a low-dimensional continuous space.

Bayesian optimization then operates in this learned space. The approach requires structural knowledge, which can come from a simulator or another mechanism for generating potentially good solutions. Variational inference estimates uncertainty in the auto-encoder’s latent space, and that uncertainty is propagated into the search to balance exploring unfamiliar candidates against exploiting promising ones.

The learned representation can bias optimization toward relevant parts of the search space, making the method suitable for transfer-learning tasks. Experiments across several application domains illustrate its utility and generality. The contribution is a way to combine available structural knowledge, learned continuous representations, and uncertainty-aware search so that optimization can work with complex candidates through a more manageable space.
icml-2018-structured-variationally-auto-.tldr: A structure-generating variational auto-encoder enables uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization over complex candidates using available structural knowledge.

paragraphs: This paper studies testing whether an undirected graphical model contains a particular combinatorial structure. Knowing that the available data theoretically contains enough information to distinguish two possibilities does not establish that an efficient algorithm can extract that information. The authors investigate this gap between statistical possibility and computational feasibility.

Using an oracle computational model, they quantify the minimum computation needed to reach information-theoretic limits. They show that tractable algorithms generally cannot attain those limits for several testing problems, including detecting cliques, nearest-neighbor graphs, or perfect matchings against an empty graph, and distinguishing a large clique from a small one. These impossibility results are framed within the specified computational model.

The authors introduce weak and strong edge densities as structural quantities that help explain when computational-statistical trade-offs arise. This connects the difficulty of inference to properties of the structures being tested. The contribution goes beyond identifying individual hard cases: it provides a structural account of why enough information for successful testing may still be insufficient for computationally tractable testing.
icml-2018-the-edge-density-barrier-compu.tldr: Oracle-model lower bounds and edge-density measures explain gaps between statistical possibility and efficient computation in graphical-model structure testing.

paragraphs: This paper connects fast stochastic gradient descent to interpolation: training over-parameterized models until empirical loss is close to zero. It studies why this regime can make optimization fast, while explicitly leaving open why interpolating solutions generalize well. For convex losses in the analyzed regime, mini-batch SGD receives an exponential convergence bound comparable to full gradient descent.

The analysis identifies a critical batch size m*. At or below this threshold, one update using m examples is nearly equivalent to m single-example updates. Above it, an update becomes nearly equivalent to a full-gradient update, producing a saturation regime. For quadratic loss, the authors derive explicit optimal batch and step sizes and characterize both regimes.

The threshold marks a limit to effective mini-batch parallelization. It is nearly independent of dataset size, which supports an O(n) computational acceleration over full gradient descent in the analysis. Experiments on real data closely follow the theory. The contribution explains how interpolation changes SGD’s optimization behavior and why increasing batch size helps only up to a problem-dependent point.
icml-2018-the-power-of-interpolation-und.tldr: Interpolation enables fast SGD convergence and creates a critical batch size beyond which additional batching provides diminishing optimization benefits.
